new_statements.quote: Existen dos tipos de acento, el acento primario obligatorio y el secundario. Se distinguen por su intensidad, y ambos pueden pronosticarse. El acento primario ["] es de mayor intensidad, siempre cae en la penúltima sílaba y tiene prioridad sobre el acento secundario. El acento secundario ['] es de menor intensidad y suele presentarse en palabras de cuatro o más sílabas, cayendo en cada dos sílabas, contando desde la primera sílaba hasta el final de la palabra. Cuando la palabra es de una sola sílaba, el acento primario cae en esta sílaba.
new_statements.translation: There are two kinds of stress, obligatory primary stress and secondary stress. They are distinguished by intensity, and both are predictable. Primary stress ["] is of greater intensity, always falls on the penultimate syllable and takes priority over secondary stress. Secondary stress ['] is of lesser intensity and usually appears in words of four or more syllables, falling on every second syllable counting from the first syllable to the end of the word. When the word has a single syllable, primary stress falls on that syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the (phonological) word; monosyllables are stressed. Secondary stresses alternate on every second syllable counting from the word-initial syllable (in words of 4+ syllables), never landing adjacent to the penult primary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second syllable from the first syllable in words of four or more syllables; in odd-syllabled words (5+) the alternation starts on syllable 1 and skips the syllable before the penult, leaving two unstressed syllables mid-word (e.g. 'ša.mur'ka.ni"sa.pa); some speakers omit secondary stress in 4-syllable words; a rarer variant places the two-syllable lapse right after the initial secondary ('ya.ča.na'ya.ni"sa.pa).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exception kanawa 'canoa' (antepenult); interrogative words often take primary stress on the final syllable (maymantá '¿adónde?'; Park & Wyss 1995:22 tie this to the suffix -tá/-tí); the eyewitness-emphasis morpheme -n often attracts primary stress to its syllable; Spanish loans may keep antepenult stress (béinte, áunke) unless glides are reanalysed; in fast speech final-vowel loss can leave phonetic final stress (čaymantá < čaymantaka); a separate freely placed emphatic 'acento de intensidad' /'/ (sec. 1.1.3) can add prominence to any syllable. Navarro 1903:90 independently: penult 'casi siempre', antepenult 'pocas veces', never final except monosyllables and interjections.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('grupo de acentos'), defined in note 2 as secondary-stress margin + primary-stress nucleus, largely coinciding with the grammatical word including suffixes (examples are fully suffixed verb forms, e.g. /tukučaškanisapa/ with penult primary). Data from Maceda (1963) and Sisa (1966-67) speakers plus Alau, Lamas, Tabaloso.
new_statements.identity_note: Powlison & Nies 1976 describe San Martín Quechua proper (sanm1289; a.k.a. Lamas/Lamista Quechua, llakwash), data from Maceda (1963) and Sisa (1966-67) with additional speakers from Alau, Lamas and Tabaloso, i.e. the Lamas and Sisa dialect zones. Park & Wyss 1995 is the same variety. Navarro 1903 describes Quechua 'según se habla en el Ucayali' (Franciscan mission lingua franca), which Glottolog Not to be confused with neighbouring Chachapoyas/Amazonas Quechua (chac1250), which has word-initial stress.

sources.locator: Notas, nota 1, p.32 (PDF p.37); restated in sec. 2.6 'Predicción de los acentos', p.30 (PDF p.35); exceptions pp.33-34
sources.note: Note 1 (p.32) and sec. 2.6 (p.30): stress predictable; primary stress always on the penult; secondary stress every second syllable counting from the first syllable in words of 4+ syllables (odd-syllable words leave two unstressed syllables before the penult); monosyllables stressed; exceptions: kanawa 'canoa', interrogatives often final-stressed (maymantá), emphatic -n, Spanish loans (véinte, áunke), fast-speech apocope. Sec. 1.1.3 (pp.15-17) describes a separate freely placed emphatic 'acento de intensidad' suprasegmental.

sources.note: p.22 NOTA: 'En el quechua de San Martín, el acento recae normalmente en la penúltima sílaba de una palabra; sin embargo, cuando se añade el sufijo -tá o -tí, el acento recae en la última sílaba.'

sources.note: Gramática quechua cap. I p.90: accent 'casi siempre en la sílaba penúltima, pocas veces en la antepenúltima, y nunca, jamás, en la última', except monosyllables and some interjections (atachái, anáu, ayáu). Describes Quechua 'según se habla en el Ucayali' (Franciscan missions).

sources.note: No explicit word-stress rule; phoneme chart only. Mentions accented interrogative allomorphs -tá ~ -tí (p.33) and fn.6 contrasts Amazonas Quechua's 'acentuación en la primera sílaba'. Bibliography lists Howkins 1972 and Powlison & Nies 1976 as the phonological descriptions.
